description:
We’re building an intuitive app/tool to model Sun and Earth positions at Moon south pole landing sites—assessing solar power potential and Earth communication windows.   

Our Plan:   

• 3D CAD/Simulation for terrain & solar/orbital visuals

• Interactive Web App for clean data browser UI   

Looking for:

• Devs (Web, Three.js/WebGL, UI/UX)

• Data/Math fans (Lunar orbital calculations)

• Designers & Pitch writers
summary:
SELENE is an interactive 3D Moon that runs in any browser from a single HTML file. It lets people explore and compare lunar landing sites using real NASA LRO LOLA terrain, live Sun and Earth positions (Astronomy Engine and JPL Horizons), and a drivable rover mode.

Users can pick from 24 landmarks, see how much sunlight and Earth visibility a site gets over 30 days, and search for sites that meet their own thresholds. They can also compare two sites across 13 mission factors. Data that isn’t built in can be loaded from CSV files or fetched from URLs, and the app marks anything it can’t measure instead of inventing values. In rover mode, an information card explains each landmark as you approach it.

Choosing where to land or build on the Moon means balancing light, communications, terrain and ice access, but the tools for this are usually specialised and hard to reach. SELENE-3D makes that analysis visual, free and easy to share, supporting education, early mission planning and public interest in lunar exploration.
details:
SELENE is an interactive 3D Moon that runs in a browser from a single HTML file, with nothing to install. It renders the Moon from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data embedded in the file. A built-in astronomy engine calculates where the Sun and Earth are at any chosen date, and terrain horizons are applied so mountains block light and Earth line of sight.

Users can:

  • Explore and inspect 24 landmarks (14 landing sites, 4 permanently shadowed regions, 6 geologic features).
  • Analyse a site to see Sun and Earth elevation, 30-day sunlight and Earth-visibility timelines, and the longest dark interval.
  • Search 120 days ahead for sites meeting a minimum sunlight and Earth-visibility threshold.
  • Compare two sites across 13 mission factors, with data added from CSV files or fetched from URLs.
  • Drive a rover over the terrain, with waypoints, auto-drive, fast travel and power and link status. When the rover nears a landmark, an information card explains it and shows coordinates, elevation, and live Sun and Earth status.

Benefits

  • Free, offline-capable for core features, and shareable as a link.
  • Turns specialised site-selection questions into something visual and immediate.
  • Transparent: it shows “Awaiting source data” instead of inventing numbers, and labels what is a built-in estimate.

Intended impact

To make early lunar site analysis accessible to students, educators, enthusiasts and early-stage mission planners, and to build public understanding of why places like the lunar poles matter: sunlight for power, line of sight to Earth, safe terrain, and access to ice.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in one self-contained file.
  • Libraries: three.js (3D rendering) and Astronomy Engine (ephemerides).
  • Data and services: NASA LRO LOLA elevation (embedded), JPL Horizons (live Sun and Earth directions), Wikipedia (optional extra text), and NASA, CNSA, ISRO and JAXA mission reports as sources for the written site summaries.
  • Hardware: only a standard computer or phone with a modern browser.
  • Development: built with AI assistance from Claude. Please add any other tools your team used.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages is a natural fit.

Creativity

  • It combines a research-style analysis tool, a driving simulator and an educational guide in one file.
  • The rover’s information cards turn exploration into discovery, with explanations that appear as you approach each site.
  • The fetch system accepts any CSV, JSON or GeoJSON source, including per-point endpoints and manifest files, so data can be added without rebuilding the app.

Factors considered

  • Honesty about data: the built-in terrain is coarse, long-window results are labelled estimates, and nothing is fabricated.
  • Accessibility: no installation, no account, and layouts that adapt to smaller screens.
  • Reliability: core features work offline, and online features fail gracefully.
  • Licensing and attribution: Wikipedia text carries its CC BY-SA credit, NASA data is credited, and site summaries were written in our own words.
  • Technical limits: browser cross-origin rules (CORS) and the fact that Moon Trek offers map tiles but no point-query API shaped what could be fetched live.
  • Scope: features were kept focused on the factors that matter most for site comparison.
